extracted: Table 4 prints, for drugs that included illicit benzodiazepines, a common cumulative odds ratio of 19.918 (95% CI 8.573 to 46.273). Its category probabilities after a positive result are 0.032, 0.701 and 0.266 for less or none, same and more; after a negative result they are 0.009, 0.334 and 0.657 (the last with 95% CI 0.091 to 0.973). Editors' calculations: odds(0.032)/odds(0.009) = 3.640 and odds(1-0.266)/odds(1-0.657) = 5.285. Allowing each probability to vary by 0.0005 gives conservative ranges of 3.391-3.918 and 5.260-5.311: they are mutually disjoint and exclude the printed common odds ratio. Methods p. 3 describes applying a logistic function to a least-square mean to obtain the two cumulative probabilities over a balanced population. Under that procedure, if the probabilities and contrast use the same proportional-odds model and covariate weights, both cumulative-odds ratios would equal the common model contrast. Averaging probabilities first is a different procedure and can give other ratios; the mismatch does not establish that the fitted coefficient is wrong. Neither a replacement common odds ratio nor a corrected subgroup ordering is identified. No fitted model or prediction code is provided in the supplied paper. The printed overall common odds ratio is 4.373 (95% CI 3.448 to 5.545), with positive-result probabilities 0.090, 0.847 and 0.063, and negative-result probabilities 0.023, 0.752 and 0.225. Note [1] announces a number of participants per model that no column gives. Note [2] lists overdose in the past 30 days among the covariates; it was asked in the baseline survey (p. 2), and no overdose or other harm outcome is analysed. Only the any-change association was the primary hypothesis: the authors made no adjustment for multiple comparisons and call all other p-values descriptive (pp. 3, 5). In Table 3, after a positive against a negative result: took turns 0.24 against 0.19, used near someone who had naloxone 0.23 against 0.15, used less 0.11 against 0.02.

extracted: The paper itself calls the follow-up one month: the abstract says the women completed a survey after one month, and the hypothesis (AM p. 3), the Methods (AM p. 4), the flow diagram (Fig. 2) and the title of Table 2 speak of one-month follow-up; the Results give the mean of 56 days, with 22.1% followed up within one month (AM p. 6). Solitary drug use and overdose were asked about the past month at both visits, unlike drug use (Methods 2.2.4). The abstract gives solitary drug use as 96% against 68%; 96% matches the baseline of all 103 women (99, 96.1%) or of the 68 who completed follow-up (95.6%) in Table 1, not the paired baseline of 94.9% among the 59 who used opioids at follow-up (Table 3).
